title: Earl Fouche and Gilbert Young as hard-to-handle sidemen
summary: Ridgley describes Fouche and Gilbert Young as good players with big heads who were hard to work with; Young started young on second cornet.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. Well we've been talking to you you know. What about Earl Fusche? Did you ever know him?

Yeah. Pretty good saxophone player. He played with me a while but he's another fella with a big head that couldn't get along with him. Thought he was going to saxophone player in town. I don't know what he'd come up in.
I think he's in California now. Yeah he left there already now.
But he went out and found I guess some saxophone players. He was pretty good here. When was he with you?

I don't know. Maybe we'll be able to tell you. Was he before Handy or? Before Handy or? I just can't get them together. Let's see. I think he was before Handy. Was it before he was with Sam Morgan or after? No, after he was with Morgan. Oh he made those records with Morgan in 27 I believe it was. So it would have to be after 27 then.
It was after Morgan because he came with our band because we were making more money in Morgan and he was glad to be with us but it was hard to get along with.
What about Albert French? Do you know him, the banjo player? Yeah I know him but he never played any of them. And what about Gilbert Young?

He played with him in a while. He got a big head until he still got it. He couldn't get along. I think when he couldn't divide, he tried to read and he couldn't play four quarters in the bar. At that way back there in slow time, all that. And he got so big I had to get rid of him.

He started with me when he was quite young, going to play second cornet. His boy had a good tone and he could make high notes and had a good drag time in his head and everything like that and I just thought maybe he made good enough. He was hard to get along with. Especially with my kind of a work I had.
